rows.stem: Which of the following is not true about enantiomers ?

options.label: B
options.text: They have the same melting or boiling point.

options.label: C
options.text: They have the same specific rotation.

options.label: D
options.text: They have the same chemical reactivity.

rows.solution:
The statement that is NOT true is that enantiomers have the same SPECIFIC ROTATION.

Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, and they differ in exactly ONE physical property: the direction in which they rotate plane polarised light. Their specific rotations are equal in MAGNITUDE but OPPOSITE in sign — one dextrorotatory, one laevorotatory.

Everything else about them is identical, because in an ordinary achiral environment the two molecules encounter no difference. They have the same density, the same melting and boiling points, the same solubility in ordinary solvents, and the same chemical reactivity towards achiral reagents.

That identity is precisely why enantiomers are so hard to separate, and why the separation must use something itself CHIRAL — a chiral reagent, a chiral solvent or an enzyme.

rows.stem: Aspirin is obtained by the acetylation of which of the following compounds ?
rows.solution:
Aspirin is obtained by acetylating SALICYLIC ACID.

Salicylic acid carries both a carboxyl group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent ring carbons. Acetic anhydride acetylates the PHENOLIC hydroxyl, leaving the carboxyl free:
\(\mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3COO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

ACETYLSALICYLIC ACID is aspirin — so that option names the product rather than the starting material, which is the trap.

The point of the acetylation is medical: free salicylic acid irritates the stomach lining badly, and masking its phenolic hydroxyl as an ester makes the drug tolerable. Salicylaldehyde has an aldehyde where the acid has a carboxyl, and phenol lacks both.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: The reactivities of the carbonyl compounds \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) (I), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) (II) and \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\) (III) towards nucleophilic addition reaction decreases in the order :
rows.solution:
Reactivity decreases in the order I > II > III, that is HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3.

Nucleophilic addition begins with a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and ALKYL GROUPS do both. Each one RELEASES electron density inductively, reducing the positive charge, and each one physically blocks the approach.

Count the alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon: methanal has NONE, ethanal has ONE, propanone has TWO. The order follows directly.

Methanal is so reactive on this count that in water it exists largely as its hydrate, and the trend explains why aldehydes generally react faster than ketones in every addition of this kind.

rows.stem: Among the following, which is the strongest base ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR OPTIONS ARE PRINTED AS DRAWN STRUCTURES, not names — a benzene ring bearing (a) \(\mathrm{H_3C}-\) and \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) para to each other, (b) \(\mathrm{O_2N}-\) and \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) para, (c) \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) alone, (d) \(-\mathrm{CH_2-NH_2}\). The option text above NAMES each compound (which the brief permits) rather than approximating the drawing, but the printed form is a figure and the crop should be attached. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The strongest base is BENZYLAMINE.

The decisive question is whether the nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised into the RING. In an ARYLamine it is — the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is spread over the ortho and para carbons and is much less available to accept a proton. Aniline, 4-methylaniline and 4-nitroaniline are all arylamines.

Benzylamine is different: its nitrogen sits on a \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) group, ONE CARBON away from the ring, and that saturated carbon breaks the conjugation completely. The lone pair stays on the nitrogen, so benzylamine behaves like an ordinary aliphatic amine.

Among the three arylamines the substituent still ranks them: 4-methylaniline is strongest, its methyl group releasing density; 4-nitroaniline is much the weakest, its nitro group withdrawing the lone pair onto its own oxygen.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives only glucose ?
rows.solution:
STARCH gives only glucose on hydrolysis.

Starch is a POLYSACCHARIDE built entirely from \(\alpha\)-glucose units — linear amylose and branched amylopectin — so however far it is hydrolysed, the only monosaccharide released is glucose.

The other three fail for different reasons. FRUCTOSE is already a monosaccharide and cannot be hydrolysed at all. LACTOSE gives glucose AND galactose; SUCROSE gives glucose AND fructose — each yields a second sugar besides glucose.

Cellulose would have served equally well as an answer, being a polymer of \(\beta\)-glucose; the difference between the two polymers lies in which anomer they are built from, not in what they hydrolyse to.

rows.stem: Which of the following vitamins is water soluble ?
rows.solution:
VITAMIN C is water soluble.

The vitamins split into two families by solubility, and the practical consequence is whether the body can store them.

WATER SOLUBLE — vitamin C and the B group — dissolve in the body's aqueous fluids, so any excess is excreted in the urine and no reserve accumulates. They must be supplied regularly in the diet, which is why scurvy appeared after only a few weeks at sea.

FAT SOLUBLE — vitamins A, D, E and K — are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue, so a reserve builds up and they need not be supplied daily. All three distractors belong to this group.

rows.stem: The unit of the rate of reaction is the same as that of the rate constant for a :
rows.solution:
Rate and rate constant carry the same units for a ZERO ORDER reaction.

For a reaction of order \(n\) the rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^n\), so
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), with units \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The two sets of units agree only when the concentration term disappears, that is when \(n = 0\) — and there \(k\) IS the rate, since \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\).

For first order the constant is \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), for second order \(\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\); neither matches the rate's \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\). The last option is simply false — the units CAN be the same, for exactly one order.

rows.stem:
Kohlrausch gave the following relation for strong electrolyte :
\(\Lambda = \Lambda_{o} - \mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\)
Which of the following equality holds true ?
rows.solution:
The equality holds as \(\mathrm{C} \longrightarrow 0\).

Read the relation itself. In \(\Lambda = \Lambda_0 - \mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\), the term \(\mathrm{A}\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is what the measured molar conductivity falls short by, and it vanishes only when the concentration vanishes.

The chemistry behind the algebra: at any finite concentration the ions are close enough to interact and to drag each other back, so they move more slowly than they otherwise would. Dilution moves them apart. At INFINITE DILUTION they move entirely independently, and that limiting value is what \(\Lambda_0\) means.

Infinite dilution cannot be reached in a flask, which is why the relation matters: for a STRONG electrolyte it lets \(\Lambda_0\) be found by plotting \(\Lambda\) against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) and extrapolating the straight line back to zero.

rows.stem: An azeotropic mixture of two liquids has a boiling point higher than either of the two liquids when it :

options.label: A
options.text: shows large negative deviation from Raoult's law.

options.label: B
options.text: shows no deviation from Raoult's law.

options.label: C
options.text: shows large positive deviation from Raoult's law.

rows.solution:
An azeotrope boiling HIGHER than either component shows a large NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law.

A negative deviation means the observed vapour pressure is LOWER than predicted, because the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are STRONGER than those between like ones — so the molecules escape less readily.

Lower vapour pressure means a HIGHER boiling point: the mixture must be heated further before it reaches atmospheric pressure. That is a MAXIMUM boiling azeotrope, and nitric acid with water is the standard case, boiling at 393.5 K at about 68% acid.

A POSITIVE deviation does the reverse and gives a minimum boiling azeotrope; a solution obeying Raoult's law is ideal and forms no azeotrope at all.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following colligative property is used to find the molar mass of proteins ?
rows.solution:
OSMOTIC PRESSURE is used to find the molar mass of proteins.

A protein has an enormous molar mass, so even a substantial mass of it dissolves to give very few moles, and every colligative effect is correspondingly tiny — the depression in freezing point would be a few thousandths of a degree, below what a thermometer can read reliably.

Osmotic pressure is the exception on three counts. Its MAGNITUDE is large and readily measured even for a very dilute solution. It is measured at ROOM TEMPERATURE, so the protein is not heated and does not denature, which the boiling point method would risk. And it uses MOLARITY rather than molality, which is the concentration a laboratory can prepare directly.

The other three options are all real colligative properties, simply too small to use here.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Among the following outermost configurations of transition metals which one shows the highest oxidation state ?
rows.solution:
The configuration showing the highest oxidation state is \(3d^5\,4s^2\).

Identify each element first: \(3d^3 4s^2\) is vanadium, \(3d^5 4s^1\) is chromium, \(3d^5 4s^2\) is MANGANESE, \(3d^6 4s^2\) is iron.

The highest state a transition metal reaches is the sum of its \(ns\) electrons and its UNPAIRED \((n-1)d\) electrons — all of them available for bonding. Manganese has five unpaired d electrons plus two \(4s\), giving \(5 + 2 = 7\), and it does reach \(+7\), in the permanganate ion.

Chromium comes closest with \(5 + 1 = 6\), reached in the dichromate ion. Vanadium manages \(+5\), and iron, whose d electrons are no longer all unpaired, does not approach \(+8\) in ordinary chemistry.

rows.stem: How many ions are produced in the solution from the complex \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\) ?
rows.solution:
THREE ions are produced.

Only what sits OUTSIDE the square brackets ionises. In \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\) the brackets enclose nickel and its six ammine ligands; the two chlorides lie outside as counter ions:
\(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-}\)

That is ONE complex cation plus TWO chloride ions — three ions in all.

Counting the six ammonia molecules as separate species would give more, but they are LIGANDS, bonded directly to the nickel, and they stay inside the coordination sphere. The number of ions is exactly what a conductivity measurement reports, and it is how Werner distinguished such compounds.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following species is not expected to be a ligand ?
rows.solution:
The AMMONIUM ION, \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\), is not expected to be a ligand.

A ligand must DONATE an electron pair to the metal, so it needs a LONE PAIR available. Ammonia has one on its nitrogen; water has two on its oxygen; carbon monoxide has one on its carbon.

In the ammonium ion that lone pair is GONE — it has already been used to bond a fourth hydrogen, which is exactly how the ion forms from ammonia. There is nothing left to donate.

Worse, the ion carries a POSITIVE charge, and a positive species is repelled by a metal cation rather than attracted to it. Ligands are typically neutral molecules or anions for that reason.

rows.stem: Which of the following is the most stable complex species ?
rows.solution:
The most stable is \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\).

The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE: it binds the metal through two of its oxygens at once, closing a five-membered CHELATE RING. Three of them close three such rings around the iron.

Chelation confers extra stability, an effect large enough to have its own name — the CHELATE EFFECT. Two reasons lie behind it: once one donor atom has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily, whereas a separate ligand would have to arrive from solution; and releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

The other three complexes all use MONODENTATE ligands — cyanide, carbon monoxide, water — so none closes a ring, however strong its individual bonds may be.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order and molecularity of a reaction are always same.
Reason (R) : Complex reactions involve a sequence of elementary reactions and the slowest step is rate determining.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Order and molecularity are NOT always the same. They coincide only for an ELEMENTARY reaction, where the single step IS the reaction — and for a complex reaction molecularity is not even defined, so the two cannot be compared at all.

The Reason is correct, and it explains exactly why. A complex reaction is a SEQUENCE of elementary steps, each possibly with its own molecularity, so the sequence as a whole has none to quote. And its observed ORDER is governed by the SLOWEST step, which may involve quite different species from the balanced equation.

Two further consequences follow: order may be zero or fractional, because it is measured; molecularity must be a whole number of at least 1, because it counts colliding species.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Electrolysis of aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) gives chlorine gas at anode instead of oxygen gas.
Reason (R) : Formation of oxygen gas at anode requires overpotential.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

At the anode the two candidates for oxidation are water and the chloride ion:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\), \(E^{\circ} = +1{\cdot}23\) V
\(2\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2e^-\), \(E^{\circ} = +1{\cdot}36\) V

On the potentials alone the LOWER value should win, so water should be oxidised and oxygen evolved. It is not — and OVERPOTENTIAL is why.

Liberating oxygen at an electrode requires a substantial EXTRA voltage beyond its thermodynamic value, because the process is kinetically sluggish; chlorine needs almost none. That extra requirement more than wipes out oxygen's \(0{\cdot}13\) V advantage, and chlorine is evolved instead.

This is the one case in the syllabus where the standard potentials alone give the wrong answer, and it is why the industrial chlor-alkali process works at all.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Nucleophilic substitution of iodoethane is easier than chloroethane.
Reason (R): Bond energy of \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond is less than \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Nucleophilic substitution of iodoethane IS easier than that of chloroethane — the Assertion holds.

But the Reason has the bond energies the wrong way round. The \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond enthalpy is about 339 kJ per mole against the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond's 238, so the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is the WEAKER of the two, not the stronger.

And that is exactly why the Assertion holds: in any nucleophilic substitution the carbon-halogen bond must break, so the weaker bond breaks more readily and the reaction is faster. Corrected, the Reason would have explained the Assertion; as written it would predict the opposite.

The bond weakens down the group because the halogen grows larger and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well — and the iodide ion is the more stable anion besides, making it the better leaving group on both counts.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem:
Assertion (A): Zinc is not regarded as a transition element.
Reason (R): In zinc, 3d orbitals are completely filled in its ground state as well as in its oxidised state.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

A TRANSITION ELEMENT is defined as one with a PARTLY FILLED d subshell in the neutral atom OR in at least one of its stable ions.

Zinc satisfies neither condition. It is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^2\) as the atom and \(3d^{10}\) as the \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) ion — completely filled in BOTH — so the definition excludes it, and the Reason states precisely the ground on which it is excluded.

The consequences follow: zinc's compounds are white rather than coloured, diamagnetic rather than paramagnetic, and confined to the \(+2\) state.

COPPER is the instructive contrast. It too is \(3d^{10}\) as the ATOM, but \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is \(3d^9\) — partly filled — so copper IS a transition element. Everything turns on the ion as well as the atom.

rows.stem:
Write the structures and IUPAC names of the products expected from the following reactions :
(a) Reaction of methanal with \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHMgBr}\) followed by hydrolysis.
(b) Reaction of phenol with conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\).
rows.solution:
(a) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and with METHANAL — the only aldehyde carrying two hydrogens there — the product after hydrolysis is a PRIMARY alcohol with one carbon more than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHMgBr}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}CH_2OH}\)

Structure: \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}CH_2{-}OH}\)
IUPAC name: 2-METHYLPROPAN-1-OL

Any other aldehyde would have given a secondary alcohol, and a ketone a tertiary one — methanal is what makes the product primary.

(b) Concentrated nitric acid nitrates phenol at all three activated positions, the hydroxyl group being strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH}\)

Structure: a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) with \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) groups at positions 2, 4 and 6.
IUPAC name: 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL, known as picric acid.

Dilute nitric acid stops at the mono-substituted stage and gives a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.

rows.stem:
A chemical reaction
\(2\mathrm{N_2O_5\,(g)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{NO_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{O_2\,(g)}\)
in gas phase was carried out in a closed vessel. The concentration of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) was found to increase by \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) in 10 seconds. Calculate :
(a) the rate of formation of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\), and
(b) the rate of consumption of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\).
rows.solution:
The data give the change in \([\mathrm{NO_2}]\) directly, so start there.

(a) RATE OF FORMATION OF \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is the rate at which its own concentration rises:
\(\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{10}\)

\(= 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

(b) RATE OF CONSUMPTION OF \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) follows from the stoichiometry. The equation shows TWO molecules of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) consumed for every FOUR of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) formed, so \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) disappears at HALF the rate at which \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) appears:
\(-\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2}{4}\,\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 5 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(= 2{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

Note what is NOT being asked. The RATE OF REACTION — the single number that describes the process regardless of which species is watched — is
\(\text{Rate} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{\Delta t} = 1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)
and each species' own rate is that number times its coefficient.

[The marking scheme labels this last quantity as the rate of FORMATION of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\), then halves it again for \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\), arriving at \(1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(6{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-5}\). Both are a factor of four below the rates the question asks for; the division by 4 belongs to the rate of REACTION, not to the rate of formation of the species itself.]

rows.stem: Define fuel cell and write its two advantages.
rows.solution:
A FUEL CELL is a galvanic cell in which the energy of COMBUSTION OF A FUEL is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy, the reactants being supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within the cell.

The hydrogen-oxygen cell used on the Apollo flights is the standard example: hydrogen is oxidised at one porous carbon electrode and oxygen reduced at the other, with aqueous potassium hydroxide between them.

TWO ADVANTAGES:

HIGH EFFICIENCY, around 70%. The chemical energy goes straight to electricity instead of passing through heat, so the cell is not limited by the Carnot efficiency that caps any heat engine — a thermal power station managing about 40% is the comparison.

POLLUTION FREE. The only product is WATER, with no oxides of carbon, nitrogen or sulphur and no particulates. On Apollo the water produced was drunk by the crew.

rows.stem:
Using \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\) values of X and Y given below, predict which is better for coating the surface of Iron to prevent corrosion and why ?
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{X}^{2+}/\mathrm{X}} = -\,2{\cdot}36\) V
\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Y}^{2+}/\mathrm{Y}} = -\,0{\cdot}14\) V
\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe}} = -\,0{\cdot}44\) V
rows.solution:
X is the better coating.

The principle is SACRIFICIAL PROTECTION: the coating metal must be MORE readily oxidised than the iron beneath it, so that it corrodes first and the iron does not.

Compare the standard reduction potentials. \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{X^{2+}/X}} = -2{\cdot}36\) V is MORE NEGATIVE than iron's \(-0{\cdot}44\) V, so X is the more easily oxidised of the two and will be attacked in preference — the iron is protected even where the coating is scratched.

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Y^{2+}/Y}} = -0{\cdot}14\) V is LESS negative than iron's, so Y is harder to oxidise than iron. A Y coating protects only as a physical barrier, and the moment it is scratched the iron becomes the anode of the pair and corrodes FASTER than it would unprotected.

This is why iron is galvanised with ZINC (\(-0{\cdot}76\) V) rather than plated with tin for structural use.

rows.stem:
(i) How are carbohydrates stored in animal body ? Mention any one organ where they are present.
(ii) What is the basic structural difference between starch and cellulose ?
rows.solution:
(i) Carbohydrates are stored in the animal body as GLYCOGEN, also called animal starch.

It is present in the LIVER and in MUSCLE, and also in the brain. When the blood sugar falls, enzymes break glycogen back down to glucose and release it.

Structurally it resembles amylopectin — a polymer of \(\alpha\)-glucose with \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linkages along the chains and \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_6}\) linkages at branch points — but it is MORE HIGHLY BRANCHED. That heavy branching is functional: many chain ends mean many places for enzymes to start, so glucose can be released quickly when it is wanted.

(ii) STARCH is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-GLUCOSE; CELLULOSE is a polymer of \(\beta\)-GLUCOSE.

The difference is the configuration at the anomeric carbon of each unit, and it has a large consequence. The \(\alpha\) linkage lets the chain coil, and human enzymes can hydrolyse it; the \(\beta\) linkage gives a straight chain that packs into rigid fibres, and we cannot digest it at all.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between :
(i) Peptide linkage and Glycosidic linkage
(ii) Nucleoside and Nucleotide
rows.solution:
(i) A PEPTIDE LINKAGE joins two AMINO ACIDS. It is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) formed when the carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, losing water — so the atom doing the joining is a NITROGEN.

A GLYCOSIDIC LINKAGE joins two MONOSACCHARIDES, through an OXYGEN atom bridging them, again with the loss of water.

One builds proteins, the other carbohydrates, and they differ in both what they join and the atom that joins it.

(ii) A NUCLEOSIDE has TWO components — a nitrogenous BASE joined to a pentose SUGAR at \(\mathrm{C_1}\).

A NUCLEOTIDE has THREE — the same base and sugar PLUS a PHOSPHATE group esterifying the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\).

The phosphate is the whole of the difference, and it is what makes the chain possible: it links the \(\mathrm{C_5}\) of one sugar to the \(\mathrm{C_3}\) of the next, building the backbone of a nucleic acid.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Carboxylic carbon is less electrophilic than Carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones.
(b) Propanal is more reactive than Propanone towards addition of \(\mathrm{HCN}\).
rows.solution:
(a) Because the carboxyl carbon is stabilised by RESONANCE with the hydroxyl oxygen.

In a carboxylic acid the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) oxygen donates a lone pair into the carbonyl group, so the carbon carries far less positive charge than a plain carbonyl carbon does. Resonance structures can be drawn placing a negative charge on the carbonyl oxygen and a positive one on the hydroxyl oxygen, with the carbon between them relieved of much of its deficiency.

An aldehyde or ketone has no such donor beside it — only hydrogen or alkyl groups, which cannot supply a lone pair.

The consequence is that a nucleophile finds little to attack in a carboxylic acid, which is why carboxylic acids do NOT give the characteristic addition reactions of the carbonyl group: no bisulphite addition, no cyanohydrin, no ammonia-derivative condensation.

(b) Because propanal's carbonyl carbon is MORE ELECTROPHILIC and LESS CROWDED.

Addition of hydrogen cyanide begins with the cyanide ion attacking that carbon, so the more positive and the more accessible it is, the faster the reaction.

Propanone carries TWO alkyl groups on its carbonyl carbon; propanal carries ONE alkyl group and a hydrogen. Each alkyl group RELEASES electron density inductively, reducing the positive charge, and each one physically blocks the nucleophile's approach — so propanone is deactivated on both counts, twice over.

Both effects run the same way, which is why aldehydes generally outrun ketones in every addition of this kind.

rows.stem:
Write the chemical equation involved in the following reactions :
(a) Carbylamine reaction
(b) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
rows.solution:
(a) CARBYLAMINE REACTION. A primary amine heated with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives an ISOCYANIDE, detected at once by its exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH(alc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R{-}NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

It is a test for PRIMARY amines only — forming the isocyanide requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens, so secondary and tertiary amines fail. It works for aromatic primary amines too.

(b) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, made acidic by the two flanking carbonyls; the anion then displaces halide from the alkyl halide in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step; and alkaline hydrolysis frees the amine.

Its value is that it gives a PURE PRIMARY amine, with no secondary or tertiary contamination. It fails for aromatic amines, since an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Aquatic animals are more comfortable in cold water in comparison to warm water.
(b) Sprinkling of salt helps in clearing the snow-covered roads in hilly areas.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the SOLUBILITY OF OXYGEN in water is HIGHER at a LOWER temperature.

Dissolving a gas is an EXOTHERMIC process, so by Le Chatelier's principle warming drives it backwards. Cold water therefore holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water at the same pressure, and aquatic animals, which breathe what is dissolved, are the better off for it.

This is why thermal pollution — warm water discharged from a power station into a river — threatens fish without adding anything toxic at all.

(b) Because the salt causes a DEPRESSION IN FREEZING POINT.

Snow and the water in contact with it form a solution once salt dissolves in it, and a solution freezes BELOW the freezing point of the pure solvent. If the depression brings the freezing point below the air temperature, the snow melts and the road clears.

The effect is COLLIGATIVE, so what matters is the number of PARTICLES: sodium chloride gives two ions per formula unit and calcium chloride three, which is why calcium chloride is used where the cold is severe.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - OH} \xrightarrow[443\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \mathrm{CH_2 = CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(b) Write the equation of the reaction for the preparation of phenol from cumene.
rows.solution:
(a) MECHANISM OF DEHYDRATION AT 443 K, in three steps.

Step 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid. This step is FAST and reversible, and its purpose is to convert the poor leaving group \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into the good one, water:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 2 — formation of the carbocation. The protonated alcohol loses water. This is the SLOW, rate determining step, since a bond breaks and a charged species is created:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — elimination of a proton. A base removes a proton from the carbon next to the positive centre, and the pair of electrons left behind forms the double bond, regenerating the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The TEMPERATURE selects the product: at 413 K a second alcohol molecule attacks the protonated one instead, and the product is ethoxyethane.

(b) PHENOL FROM CUMENE, in two steps. Cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, and treating that with dilute acid cleaves it:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{O_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

The economics of the route rest on the by-product: both halves of the cumene molecule end up as something worth selling, phenol and acetone, which is why this is the industrial method.

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2 + NaOH}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}} \mathrm{C}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{C}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Heating benzoic acid with ammonia gives the ammonium salt and then, on further heating, the AMIDE:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide

Bromine with alkali is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, which converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises it, and the salt SURVIVES at that temperature because the ring delocalises the positive charge:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

(ii) Potassium cyanide substitutes for the bromide, giving the NITRILE, and the carbon count rises from two to three:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\), propanenitrile

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces a nitrile all the way to a PRIMARY AMINE, the carbon count unchanged:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\), propan-1-amine

Nitrous acid at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises this ALIPHATIC amine, and the salt so formed is unstable even at that temperature — it loses nitrogen at once and the cation picks up water:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\), propan-1-ol

The two sequences are a lesson in the difference between aliphatic and aromatic diazotisation: the same reagent preserves one substrate's diazonium salt and destroys the other's.

rows.stem:
How will you convert the following :
(i) Aniline to p-bromoaniline
(ii) Ethanoic acid to methanamine
(iii) Butanenitrile to 1-aminobutane
rows.solution:
(i) ANILINE TO p-BROMOANILINE, in three steps — and the first is PROTECTION.

Bromine water alone would give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, because the amino group is so strongly activating. Acetylating it first MODERATES that activation, so only one bromine goes on and it goes para:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]{\mathrm{Br_2}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\)

(ii) ETHANOIC ACID TO METHANAMINE, in two steps. Count the carbons: TWO in, ONE out, and that loss is the signature of the Hofmann degradation.
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\)

(iii) BUTANENITRILE TO 1-AMINOBUTANE, in one step. Here the carbon count is UNCHANGED — four in, four out — so the nitrile is simply REDUCED rather than degraded:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CN} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)

Counting carbons before choosing a method is what separates (ii) from (iii).

rows.stem:
\(0{\cdot}3\) g of acetic acid (M = 60 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) dissolved in 30 g of benzene shows a depression in freezing point equal to \(0{\cdot}45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Calculate the percentage association of acid if it forms a dimer in the solution.
(Given : \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for benzene = \(5{\cdot}12\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Acetic acid DIMERISES in benzene, so fewer particles are present than the formula suggests and the van't Hoff factor comes out BELOW 1.

Step 1 — the observed factor. Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{i\,K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = i \times 5{\cdot}12 \times \dfrac{0{\cdot}3}{60} \times \dfrac{1000}{30}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = i \times 0{\cdot}8533\)

\(i = 0{\cdot}527\)

Step 2 — degree of association. Two molecules combine into one dimer, so \(n = 2\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1 - i}{1 - \frac{1}{n}} = \dfrac{1 - 0{\cdot}527}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}473}{0{\cdot}5}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}946\)

Percentage association \(= 94{\cdot}6\%\)

The sign of the deviation is the check on the whole calculation. Association REDUCES the particle count, so \(i < 1\) and the observed depression is SMALLER than the formula predicts. Dissociation would have done the opposite.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a reaction doubles when temperature changes from \(27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Calculate energy of activation for the reaction.
(R = \(8{\cdot}314\) J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(Given : log 2 = \(0{\cdot}3010\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}4771\), log 4 = \(0{\cdot}6021\))
rows.solution:
Two rate constants at two temperatures are related by the Arrhenius equation in its two-point form:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]\)

The rate DOUBLES, so \(k_2/k_1 = 2\) and \(\log 2 = 0{\cdot}3010\). Convert the temperatures: \(27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 300\) K and \(37\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 310\) K:
\(0{\cdot}3010 = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303 \times 8{\cdot}314}\left[\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{310}\right]\)

The bracket is \(\dfrac{310 - 300}{300 \times 310} = \dfrac{10}{93000}\), so
\(E_a = \dfrac{0{\cdot}3010 \times 19{\cdot}147 \times 300 \times 310}{10}\)

\(E_a = 53598\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is about \(53{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note how ordinary the result is: a ten-degree rise doubling the rate near room temperature corresponds to an activation energy of around 50 kJ per mole, which is why that rule of thumb holds for so many reactions.

rows.stem:
Write the structure of product when D-Glucose reacts with the following : (any three)
(a) \(\mathrm{HI}\)
(b) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
(d) \(\mathrm{HCN}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN IODIDE and red phosphorus on prolonged heating, every oxygen is stripped out and the product is N-HEXANE:
\(\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3}\)
The STRAIGHT chain is the point: it proves glucose's six carbons are joined in an unbranched chain.

(b) WITH CONCENTRATED NITRIC ACID, a strong oxidising agent, BOTH ends are oxidised — the aldehyde at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and the primary alcohol at \(\mathrm{C_6}\) — giving SACCHARIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{HOOC{-}(CHOH)_4{-}COOH}\)

(c) WITH BROMINE WATER, a MILD oxidising agent, only the ALDEHYDE is attacked, giving GLUCONIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{HOCH_2{-}(CHOH)_4{-}COOH}\)
That specificity is what makes this reaction the proof of the aldehyde group; the contrast with (b) establishes the primary alcohol separately.

(d) WITH HYDROGEN CYANIDE the carbonyl adds a cyanide, giving the CYANOHYDRIN with SEVEN carbons:
\(\mathrm{CH(OH)(CN){-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH}\)
That this nucleophilic addition works at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a carbonyl group.

rows.stem: What happens when bromobenzene is treated with \(\mathrm{Mg}\) in the presence of dry ether ?
rows.context: The polarity of \(\mathrm{C - X}\) bond of alkyl halides is responsible for their nucleophilic substitution, elimination and their reaction with metal atoms to form organometallic compounds. Alkyl halides are prepared by the free radical halogenation of alkanes, addition of halogen acids to alkenes, replacement of \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of alcohols with halogens using phosphorus halides, thionyl chloride or halogen acids. Aryl halides are prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes. Nucleophilic substitution reactions are categorised into \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) on the basis of their kinetic properties. Chirality has a profound role in understanding the \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) mechanism.
rows.solution:
A GRIGNARD REAGENT is formed — PHENYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}\):
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} + \mathrm{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}\)

The magnesium inserts itself into the carbon-halogen bond. Because magnesium is far less electronegative than carbon, the carbon ends up carrying a large partial NEGATIVE charge and behaves as a carbanion — which is what makes these reagents such powerful nucleophiles and bases.

The ether is essential in two ways: it is APROTIC, so it has no acidic hydrogen to destroy the reagent, and its oxygen lone pairs coordinate to the magnesium and keep the reagent in solution. The conditions must be strictly ANHYDROUS, since water would protonate the carbanion and give benzene.

rows.stem:
Which compound in each of the following pairs will react faster in \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) reaction with \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ?
(1) \(\mathrm{CH_2 = CH - CH_2 - Cl}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH_2 - CH_2 - Cl}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C - Cl}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)
rows.context: The polarity of \(\mathrm{C - X}\) bond of alkyl halides is responsible for their nucleophilic substitution, elimination and their reaction with metal atoms to form organometallic compounds. Alkyl halides are prepared by the free radical halogenation of alkanes, addition of halogen acids to alkenes, replacement of \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of alcohols with halogens using phosphorus halides, thionyl chloride or halogen acids. Aryl halides are prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes. Nucleophilic substitution reactions are categorised into \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) on the basis of their kinetic properties. Chirality has a profound role in understanding the \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) mechanism.
rows.solution:
(1) ALLYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\), reacts faster.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the CARBOCATION forms. Allyl chloride's halogen sits on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so the cation left behind is delocalised over TWO carbons by resonance. n-Propyl chloride gives a plain primary cation with no such help.

(2) tert-BUTYL CHLORIDE, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Cl}\), reacts faster.

It is TERTIARY, and its cation is stabilised by electron release from three methyl groups. Methyl chloride would have to form the METHYL cation, which has nothing at all to stabilise it and is the least stable carbocation there is — so methyl halides essentially never react by this route.

Both pairs illustrate the same rule from two directions: whatever stabilises the carbocation speeds an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction up.

rows.stem:
Write the equations for the preparation of 1-iodobutane from
(1) 1-chlorobutane
(2) but-1-ene.
rows.context: The polarity of \(\mathrm{C - X}\) bond of alkyl halides is responsible for their nucleophilic substitution, elimination and their reaction with metal atoms to form organometallic compounds. Alkyl halides are prepared by the free radical halogenation of alkanes, addition of halogen acids to alkenes, replacement of \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of alcohols with halogens using phosphorus halides, thionyl chloride or halogen acids. Aryl halides are prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes. Nucleophilic substitution reactions are categorised into \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) on the basis of their kinetic properties. Chirality has a profound role in understanding the \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) mechanism.
rows.solution:
(1) FROM 1-CHLOROBUTANE — the FINKELSTEIN reaction, an exchange of one halogen for another:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The solvent is what drives it. Sodium iodide is SOLUBLE in acetone while sodium chloride is NOT, so the chloride precipitates out and the equilibrium is pulled across — an exchange that would otherwise not favour the product.

(2) FROM BUT-1-ENE, in two steps. Adding hydrogen bromide in the presence of PEROXIDE gives ANTI-Markovnikov addition, putting the halogen on the TERMINAL carbon:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)

Then exchange the bromide for iodide as before:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I}\)

The peroxide is essential: without it the addition would be Markovnikov and the halogen would land on the SECOND carbon, giving the wrong isomer.

rows.stem:
Write the structure of the major products in each of the following reactions :
(1) \(\mathrm{CH_3 - CH(Br) - CH_3} + \mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{Ethanol}}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{Anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}}\)
rows.context: The polarity of \(\mathrm{C - X}\) bond of alkyl halides is responsible for their nucleophilic substitution, elimination and their reaction with metal atoms to form organometallic compounds. Alkyl halides are prepared by the free radical halogenation of alkanes, addition of halogen acids to alkenes, replacement of \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of alcohols with halogens using phosphorus halides, thionyl chloride or halogen acids. Aryl halides are prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes. Nucleophilic substitution reactions are categorised into \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) on the basis of their kinetic properties. Chirality has a profound role in understanding the \(\mathrm{S_N^{1}}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N^{2}}\) mechanism.
rows.solution:
(1) KOH in ETHANOL with heat supplies ALKOXIDE ions, which are strong BASES but poor nucleophiles, so they attack a \(\beta\) HYDROGEN and the halide is ELIMINATED:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(Br){-}CH_3} + \mathrm{KOH(alc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3{-}CH{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The major product is PROPENE. Both \(\beta\) carbons here are equivalent methyls, so only one alkene is possible; aqueous KOH would have given propan-2-ol instead, by substitution.

(2) Chlorobenzene with ethanoyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride is a Friedel-Crafts ACYLATION. The chlorine on the ring is DEACTIVATING — it withdraws density inductively — but ORTHO, PARA DIRECTING, because its lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance and raises the density at those positions.

The major product is 1-(4-CHLOROPHENYL)ETHANONE — a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(-\mathrm{COCH_3}\) PARA to each other. The para isomer predominates because the ortho position is crowded by the chlorine already there.

rows.stem: When a coordination compound \(\mathrm{NiCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O}\) is mixed with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, 2 moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the complex and secondary valency for Nickel ion.
rows.context: Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion.
rows.solution:
Two moles of silver chloride per mole of complex means TWO chlorides are free in solution, outside the coordination sphere — so neither is a ligand, and the six water molecules must fill all six coordination positions.

STRUCTURAL FORMULA: \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\)

SECONDARY VALENCY: 6. Werner's secondary valency is the COORDINATION NUMBER, the count of donor atoms bonded directly to the metal — six water molecules, each monodentate, give six, and the geometry is octahedral.

The primary valency is 2, matching nickel's \(+2\) oxidation state and the two chlorides outside.

rows.stem: Write the IUPAC name of the ionisation isomer of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Cl}\).
rows.context: Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion.
rows.solution:
IONISATION ISOMERS exchange a LIGAND inside the coordination sphere for a COUNTER ION outside it. In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Cl}\) the sulphate is the ligand and the chloride the counter ion; its isomer swaps them:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\)

Naming it: five ammine ligands are neutral and the chlorido ligand gives \(-1\), so against a sulphate of \(-2\) outside, cobalt must be \(+3\):
PENTAAMMINECHLORIDOCOBALT(III) SULPHATE

The two are easily told apart, because they give DIFFERENT ions in solution. This one releases sulphate, so it gives a white precipitate with barium chloride; the original releases chloride, so it gives one with silver nitrate. Each fails the other's test.

rows.stem:
Using Valence Bond Theory, predict the geometry and magnetic nature of :
(1) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\)
[Atomic number : Ni = 28, Fe = 26]
rows.context: Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion.
rows.solution:
(1) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\). Nickel is atomic number 28, and here it is in the ZERO oxidation state — carbon monoxide is a neutral ligand and the complex carries no charge — so the atom is \(3d^8 4s^2\).

Carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\) with every electron paired and no \(3d\) orbital free. Bonding must then use the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\) orbitals: hybridisation \(sp^3\).

GEOMETRY: TETRAHEDRAL. MAGNETIC NATURE: DIAMAGNETIC, with no unpaired electron.

(2) \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\). Iron is atomic number 26; six cyanides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\).

Cyanide is a STRONG FIELD ligand and pairs those electrons into the three lower orbitals as \(t_{2g}^5\), freeing TWO inner \(3d\) orbitals; with the \(4s\) and \(4p\) these give \(d^2sp^3\).

GEOMETRY: OCTAHEDRAL. MAGNETIC NATURE: PARAMAGNETIC, with ONE unpaired electron left over, \(\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M.

rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(1) Low spin tetrahedral complexes are not formed.
(2) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an inner orbital complex whereas \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) is an outer orbital complex.
[Atomic number : Co = 27, Ni = 28]
rows.context: Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion.
rows.solution:
(1) Because \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}}\) IS NEVER LARGE ENOUGH to force the electrons to pair.

A tetrahedral field splits the d orbitals only weakly, for two reasons: there are only FOUR ligands rather than six, and none of them points directly at a d orbital. The result is that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}}\) is about four-ninths of \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) for the same metal and ligands.

That figure is essentially always BELOW the pairing energy. With \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} < \mathrm{P}\) the electrons always prefer to occupy the upper orbitals singly rather than pair up, so tetrahedral complexes are high spin and low spin ones are hardly ever seen.

(2) Because the two IONS differ in how many d electrons they have, not in the ligand.

\(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a strong field ligand and pairs all six into the lower set as \(t_{2g}^6\), which FREES TWO INNER \(3d\) orbitals — so bonding uses \(d^2sp^3\) and the complex is an INNER ORBITAL one.

\(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). Eight electrons in five orbitals must sit as three pairs and two singles WHATEVER the ligand does — there are simply not enough vacancies to pair them further, so no inner \(3d\) orbital can be freed. Bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set, giving \(sp^3d^2\) and an OUTER ORBITAL complex.

The same ligand therefore gives opposite answers, because \(d^8\) is the one configuration where the field strength cannot change the count.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(1) Transition metals form complex compounds.
(2) The \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mn}}\) value for manganese is highly negative whereas \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}/\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}}\) is highly positive.
(3) \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) ion is unstable in aqueous solution.
(ii) Write the equations involved in the preparation of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) from Pyrolusite ore \((\mathrm{MnO_2})\).
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because of their SMALL SIZE, HIGH IONIC CHARGE and the availability of VACANT d ORBITALS of suitable energy.

A small, highly charged cation exerts a strong electrostatic pull on a ligand's lone pair, and the vacant d orbitals give it somewhere to accept that pair. Transition metals also have variable oxidation states, so the same element can form complexes in several charge states.

(2) Both values are set by the stability of \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell.

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) is highly NEGATIVE because manganese metal gives up two electrons readily to REACH that stable ion, so the metal is easily oxidised.

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}}\) is highly POSITIVE for the same reason seen from the other side: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) would GAIN that stability by picking up one electron, so it is strongly inclined to be reduced.

(3) Because \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) DISPROPORTIONATES in aqueous solution:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The driving force is hydration energy. \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) carries twice the charge on a smaller ion, so it is hydrated far more strongly than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\), and that extra energy more than pays for the second ionisation. In the SOLID state, with no water to do the hydrating, copper(I) compounds are perfectly stable.

(ii) PREPARATION OF POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE FROM PYROLUSITE, in two stages.

Stage 1 — fusion with alkali in the presence of air, raising manganese from \(+4\) to \(+6\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Stage 2 — disproportionation of the green manganate in acid, manganese going both up to \(+7\) and down to \(+4\):
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Industrially the second stage is done by ELECTROLYTIC oxidation instead, which converts all the manganate rather than only two-thirds.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(i) Identify the following :
(1) Transition metal of 3d series that exhibits only one oxidation state.
(2) Transition metal of 3d series that acts as a strong reducing agent in +2 oxidation state in aqueous solution.
(ii) Complete and balance the following equations :
(1) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H}^{+} + 6\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \longrightarrow\)
(2) \(\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\)
(iii) What is Misch metal ? Write its one use.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) SCANDIUM exhibits only one oxidation state, \(+3\).

Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\). Losing all three electrons gives \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), which has the argon configuration — an empty \(3d\) subshell with nothing further to give. Its compounds are white and diamagnetic in consequence.

(2) CHROMIUM acts as a strong reducing agent in the \(+2\) state.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is \(3d^4\), and losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral aqueous environment the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Chromium(II) therefore gives that electron up eagerly; \(E^{\circ}\) for the couple is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V, negative enough that chromium(II) reduces even water.

(ii)(1) Dichromate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) in acid, chromium falling from \(+6\) to \(+3\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Six electrons change hands: two chromiums take three each, six iron(II) ions give up one each.

(2) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it, manganese ending in two different oxidation states:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

(iii) MISCH METAL is an ALLOY of a lanthanoid with iron — roughly 95% lanthanoid and 5% iron, with traces of sulphur, carbon, calcium and aluminium.

USE: it is PYROPHORIC, so it is used in making BULLETS AND SHELLS and as the flint of a cigarette lighter.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) An organic compound (X) having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) can show various properties depending on its structures. Draw each of the structures if it
(1) gives positive iodoform test.
(2) shows Cannizzaro's reaction.
(3) reduces Tollens' reagent and has a chiral carbon.
(ii) Write the reaction involved in the following :
(1) Wolff-Kishner reduction
(2) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction
rows.solution:
(i) The formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) has one degree of unsaturation, which the carbonyl group uses up — so every structure is a saturated five-carbon aldehyde or ketone.

(1) POSITIVE IODOFORM TEST requires a METHYL group attached to the carbonyl carbon:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2{-}CO{-}CH_3}\), pentan-2-one

(2) CANNIZZARO'S REACTION requires an aldehyde with NO \(\alpha\)-HYDROGEN, since an aldehyde that has one undergoes aldol instead. The carbon next to the carbonyl must therefore be fully substituted:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO}\), 2,2-dimethylpropanal

(3) REDUCES TOLLENS' REAGENT means an ALDEHYDE; a chiral carbon means one carbon must carry four different groups:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}CH(CH_3){-}CHO}\), 2-methylbutanal
Its second carbon holds a methyl, an ethyl, a hydrogen and the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group — four different things.

(ii)(1) WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), in two stages — hydrazine condenses with it to the hydrazone, and heating with a strong base expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N{-}NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

(2) HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY REACTION halogenates a carboxylic acid at its \(\alpha\) position, with a little red phosphorus as catalyst:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CH_2{-}COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{X_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{R{-}CH(X){-}COOH}\) where \(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{Cl}\) or \(\mathrm{Br}\)

The phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl halide, which enolises far more readily than the acid itself, and it is the enol that the halogen attacks.

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem:
(i) How can you convert each of the following compounds to Benzoic acid ?
(1) Acetophenone
(2) Ethylbenzene
(3) Bromobenzene
(ii) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their property as indicated :
(1) \(\mathrm{O_2N - CH_2 - COOH}\), \(\mathrm{F - CH_2 - COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CN - CH_2COOH}\)
(Acidic character)
(2) Ethanal, Propanal, Butanone, Propanone
(Reactivity in nucleophilic addition reactions)
rows.solution:
(i)(1) ACETOPHENONE TO BENZOIC ACID. Alkaline permanganate cleaves the side chain right down to the carboxyl group, and acidification frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

(2) ETHYLBENZENE TO BENZOIC ACID, by the same reagent. The whole ethyl side chain is cut back to a single carboxyl carbon, the second carbon being lost entirely:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

(3) BROMOBENZENE TO BENZOIC ACID, by way of a Grignard reagent, which ADDS a carbon:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

The first two conversions SHORTEN the side chain; the third BUILDS one. Counting carbons shows at once which kind of step is needed.

(ii)(1) Increasing acidic character:
\(\mathrm{F{-}CH_2{-}COOH} < \mathrm{CN{-}CH_2{-}COOH} < \mathrm{O_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH}\)

All three substituents withdraw electron density and so stabilise the carboxylate ion, strengthening the acid; the order follows how strongly each one pulls. The NITRO group is much the most powerful, withdrawing by resonance as well as inductively. Cyano and fluoro are closer, with the cyano group slightly the stronger puller — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 2.47 against fluoroethanoic acid's 2.59, against nitroethanoic acid's 1.68.

[The marking scheme accepts either this order or one placing the cyano compound first; the measured \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values support the order given here.]

(2) Increasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition:
BUTANONE < PROPANONE < PROPANAL < ETHANAL

Reactivity falls as the carbonyl carbon is made less positive and more crowded, and each ALKYL group does both. Ethanal has one methyl; propanal has one ethyl, slightly bulkier and more electron releasing. Propanone has TWO methyls; butanone has a methyl and an ethyl, the bulkiest pairing of the four.

rows.stem:
(a) Calculate the emf of the following cell at \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :
\(\mathrm{Zn\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{H}^{+}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{H_2\,(g)}\,(1\ \mathrm{bar}),\ \mathrm{Pt\,(s)}\)
[Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\) V, \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H_2}} = 0{\cdot}00\) V, log 10 = 1]
(b) State Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions. Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease with dilution ?
rows.solution:
(a) Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so zinc is oxidised and the hydrogen electrode on the right is the cathode.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}00 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid zinc does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10^{3}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0885\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}671\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note the SQUARED term: \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), so the quotient is \(10^{3}\), not 10. The hydrogen ion's coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation carries through as an exponent in the Nernst quotient.

(b) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS states that the LIMITING molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and anion, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)

At infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid.

WHY CONDUCTIVITY FALLS ON DILUTION. Conductivity is the conductance of a FIXED VOLUME — the solution held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. Diluting puts FEWER IONS PER UNIT VOLUME into that space, so fewer charge carriers are available to carry the current, and the conductivity falls.

MOLAR conductivity behaves the opposite way, RISING on dilution, because it counts the ions from a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume.
